_comment: Domain knowledge that no general-purpose embedding model carries.
An advisor asking for 'address proof' wants the electricity bill, but nothing in the bill's
text is distributionally close to that phrase: it talks about meter readings and direct
debits. Five embedding models were measured on this corpus (all-MiniLM-L6-v2,
multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-cos-v1, msmarco-MiniLM-L6-cos-v5, e5-small-v2, bge-small-en-v1.5) and all
five ranked the bill 13th or worse for that query while ranking every other probe first.
The association is procedural knowledge about which documents evidence what, so it is supplied
explicitly here rather than hoped for from the model.
A query reaches a rule by meaning, not by containing one of its phrases: each rule's paraphrases and
its concept name are embedded once at startup with the model the semantic arm searches with, and a
query fires the rule when its vector comes within search.concept-floor of one of them and within
search.concept-floor-ratio of the best rule's score — the second number is what stops 'proof of
address' dragging 'evidence of identity' in. So 'documents that show where the client lives' reaches
the address rule though none of its words appear here. Paraphrases are examples, not a list to
complete: state the requirement the way an advisor would, avoid words every query about a person
carries — 'client' on its own pulled six unrelated queries towards a rule, pronouns ('what he owes',
'her investments') and acronyms ('photo ID') did the same — add one when a real query shows up in the
search log with concepts=[] and should not have, then run ConceptFloorTest and read its tables.
Which requirements get a rule is decided by the vocabulary-gap test, from what the satisfying document
type actually says: a CRS self-certification says 'tax residence', so the semantic arm finds it unaided
and there is no rule; a Land Registry title register says 'proprietor', never 'ownership', so there is
one. Requirements enumerated from the sources and failing the test (no rule): tax residency,
authority conferred by a letter of authority or mandate (they say 'authorise'), employment status,
marital status, health, knowledge and experience, objectives and attitude to risk, safeguarded pension
benefits, PEP screening. Dependants passed the test but was measured out: its phrasings sat at 0.77 of
the liabilities rule's and a birth certificate's own words are 'certified copy of an entry'.
Expansions are the document types a UK adviser's file holds as evidence for the requirement, named
the way the regulator or an adviser names them, so they generalise to any firm's file. Membership
comes from the governing text and adviser practice; order is how commonly a client file holds the
type. The seeded demo corpus decides none of this — it is twenty documents and lacks most of these
types — so 'reaches nothing seeded' is a fact about the seed, never a reason to drop, move or reword
an entry. EvidenceFixtureTest holds one short synthetic document per type the seed lacks and asserts
that each probe places its own document on the semantic arm's page: that is what 'the probe is
right' means here. One listed miss: 'pension statement' loses the seeded scheme statement to a
suitability report whose title is about pensions.
Only the first four expansions of a rule run for a query naming one concept, and two per rule for a
query naming two (MAX_PROBES in QueryExpander: a query is one probe and the ceiling is five). The
later entries are still the firm's accepted list — raising the ceiling is a code change and one more
vector scan per probe (about 7 ms) — so the order decides which run today.
Sources, read in their current text. Address: JMLSG Guidance Part I (June 2023, revised August 2025)
5.3.75 — 'Current council tax demand letter, or statement'; 'Recent evidence of entitlement to a state
or local authority-funded benefit' (including a pension — the DWP's document is an award letter); a document from 'a regulated utility
company' — and 5.3.76 — 'current bank statements, or credit/debit card statements, issued by a
regulated financial sector firm in the UK, or utility bills'; a mortgage statement and HMRC
correspondence are on the seeded firm's own accepted list and a tenancy agreement on Onfido's
proof-of-address list, none of them named by JMLSG. Identity: 5.3.75's photographic list — 'Valid
passport', 'Valid photocard driving licence (full or provisional)', 'National Identity card', 'Firearms
certificate or shotgun licence' — and 5.3.90's control of 'requiring copy documents to be certified by
an appropriate person'. Income: FCA MCOB 11.6.13G(1) 'Examples of evidence of income ... are payslips
and bank statements', 11.6.9G(5) 'payslips, bank statements or tax returns', 11.6.15G(2) 'a pension
statement'; the P60 is HMRC's end-of-year statement of salary and tax, which gov.uk names 'as proof of
your income if you apply for a loan or a mortgage'; an employment contract is lender practice for a new
or probationary job. Authority to act: MLR 2017 reg 28(10) — 'verify that A is authorised to act on the
customer's behalf' — and Mental Capacity Act 2005 s.9 (a lasting power of attorney confers authority
only once 'registered in accordance with Schedule 1'), s.16(2)(b) (the court-appointed 'deputy' —
gov.uk: 'you'll get a court order saying what you can and cannot do'), the enduring power of attorney
(gov.uk: usable if 'made and signed before October 1, 2007', to be registered 'when the donor starts to
lose or has lost their mental capacity'), JMLSG 5.3.75's 'grant of probate' for executors, and the general power
of attorney under the Powers of Attorney Act 1971, whose form appoints an attorney without the word 'authority'. Source
of funds and wealth: JMLSG 5.5.32 — 'a copy of the relevant will', 'evidence of conveyancing' — 5.5.6 —
'inheritance, divorce settlement, property sale' — and Annex 5-III/IV, which verifies wealth 'by reference to VAT
and income tax returns, copies of audited accounts, pay slips, public deeds'; the death certificate that opens
an estate file is adviser practice, not text. A record of a home visit is on the address rule because JMLSG
5.3.76 says a staff record of one may corroborate residence. Beneficial ownership: MLR 2017 reg 28(4) —
'identify the beneficial owner' and 'understand the ownership and control structure' — and reg 5's
'more than 25% of the shares or voting rights'; the register of people with significant control is
Companies Act 2006 Part 21A. Property ownership: lender and conveyancing practice; gov.uk describes
the title register as showing 'who owns it', while the register itself says 'proprietor'. Assets,
liabilities, expenditure: COBS 9A.2.7R — 'the source and extent of their regular income, their assets,
including liquid assets, investments and real property, and their regular financial commitments';
MCOB 11.6.11G(1) — 'credit commitments such as secured and unsecured loans and credit cards; hire
purchase agreements; child maintenance'; 11.6.13G(2) — corroborate commitments 'by making a credit
reference agency search or checking credit card or bank statements'; 11.6.10R(2) — 'council tax;
buildings insurance; ground rent and service charge for leasehold properties'. Repayment strategy: MCOB
11.6.41R(1)(a) — 'evidence that the customer will have in place a clearly understood and credible
repayment strategy' — and 11.6.45G — 'regular deposits into a savings or investment product', the sale
of another property.
The four financial-situation rules (income, assets, liabilities, expenditure) and the two whose
evidence is the same documents (repayment strategy, property ownership) are near-synonyms in this
embedding space: their exact phrasings sit at 0.70–0.73 of each other and their natural paraphrases
ride each other in within the 0.75 ratio. ConceptFloorTest prints the matrix and allows the riders
inside that cluster; the ratio is not lowered for them. The resolution is a hierarchy of rules, not a
broader phrasing — docs/search-design.md, 'Where the lexicon comes from'.
These lists are configuration, not something a model could learn, because the texts set a standard
and leave the list to the firm. JMLSG 5.3.112 says the guidance 'does not require that in all cases a
customer's address should be verified', and Part I sets no numeric recency for an identity or address
document — only 'current' and 'recent' — where the seeded onboarding checklist wants one 'dated within
the last three months'; that checklist refuses the mobile phone bill which Onfido's proof-of-address
list (18 of the 78 document types in its public API specification) accepts, and takes a national
identity card 'issued by an EEA state' only, a restriction 5.3.77 allows. Two firms reading the same
text produce two lists; this file holds one firm's.
Two requirements enumerated and rejected that no list carries: MCOB 11.6.2R assesses whether 'the customer (and
any guarantor' can pay — a guarantor's evidence is the income rule's documents in another name, and a deed
of guarantee is titled with the requirement; COBS 19.1.1CR(5) wants evidence that a client understands
transfer risks, which is the firm's own record and no document type.
'life cover paid on death' shipped in the first version and was removed on the texts, not on the
seed: nothing in JMLSG, COBS or MCOB makes life cover an evidentiary requirement — COBS 9.2.1R's
demands-and-needs test is advice content — so it encoded what a policy pays, not which document
evidences what. Its golden query stays and is rank 1 without it.
Expansions widen the semantic arm only. The lexical arm exists to match exact tokens, and OR-ing
extra terms into it would cost precision for recall the semantic arm already provides; the sparse arm
was measured with the probes and without and they changed no rank, only page length.
